Getting Started¶

This guide is meant to get new users on their way to use MOrPy.

1. Install¶

Follow the “Installation Instructions” section in the README.md file.

2. How to use MOrPy¶

2.1 Preparing and running a single model¶

The instructions to prepare and run a single model are provided in the example prepare_and_run_single_model.ipynb. The example notebook option_explorer.ipynb shows how to use morpy to explore and consult MESA’s many inlist options without having to dig for them in the MESA installation directory.

2.2 Setting up and running a grid of MESA models¶

As alluded to in the project’s README.md, there are two ways to run multiple MESA models in parallel with MOrPy.

The “local” method (backend) uses Python’s built-in concurrent.futures functionality to spawn multiple threads to compute models in parallel. This method is referred to as “local” since it only works on a single-node setup, i.e. a single laptop, desktop, or node of a compute cluster. The advantage of using the local backend is that it can be run from within a Jupyter notebook, as shown in the example run_a_grid.ipynb.

The “mpi” backend uses mpi4py to spawn multiple separate processes, each computing a MESA model. The advantage of the mpi backend is that it uses MPI (Message Passing Interface), which works both on single-node and multi-node processes. In other words, this backend is ideal for large grid computations on compute clusters. A downside of this backend is that it cannot be run from a Jupyter notebook and instead needs to be run from a regular Python script. This makes the setup of the grid (grid parameters, inlist setup etc.) somewhat less easy. Therefore, we recommend using the option_explorer.ipynb and/or a Jupyter notebook for the setup of the grid, and copying this over to the Python script afterwards.

Apart from this, the mpi backend is more tricky to set up, since the MPI processes (= “ranks”) do not communicate automatically. Please follow the example run_a_grid_with_mpi4py.py closely when creating your own script to make sure the work is distributed and the information is shared correctly over the ranks.

2.3 Status and termination¶

A big part of running model grids is keeping track of how the computations are progressing and being able to intervene when necessary. The status module of MOrPy provides a function to print the status of any models that are (1) running and (2) registered in a designated database file (see “Tracking” in the examples mentioned above.)

When you launched a model or a grid of models (see the difference between “launching” and “running” in the examples above), you can use the print_grid_status() function within the same Python session to consult the status of the grid.

However, if you ran a model or grid (in a blocking way) and/or the original Python session is inaccessible or closed, you can still consult the grid status from another Python session. To make life easier, the cli module defines a CLI command to print the status of the grid if you provide the location of the database file. Simply load the morpy environment (see “Installation Instructions” in README.md) and run

morpy_status <PATH_TO_PROJECT_DIR> <DATABASE_FILE_NAME> <REFRESH SECONDS>

(see the run_grid_* examples for more details.)

If, for some reason, you wish to terminate the grid computations prematurely and you still have access to the Python session that launched the computations, you can use the grid_run module’s stop_grid() function. Similar to the status function, there also exists a CLI command to do so, namely

morpy_stop <PATH_TO_PROJECT_DIR> <DATABASE_FILE_NAME>

2.4 Timeout and restarts¶

Some systems, such as compute clusters, have limits on how long a certain computation can run (e.g. 24 hours). To avoid your grid or model computations to be cut off abruptly, the MOrPy run/launch functions have a timeout option, in which you can specify after how much time the process should terminate (in seconds.) At this point, models will be flagged as “restart” and will be restarted again from their latest photos file. Depending on the chosen RestartPolicy, defined in the grid_run module and used in the run_a_grid_with_mpi4py.py example, MOrPy can also pick up and restart models flagged as “failed”.

Specifically, when a model is terminated before any photo files are written and is labelled as a “restart”, it will fail upon restart of the grid and be flagged as “failed”. Upon the next restart, these failed models will be picked up again and restarted from the beginning (although this can be disabled with the RestartPolicy.)

To be able to use this functionality efficiently, the photo_interval option, part of the controls namelist should be sufficiently low (the exact number depends on the duration of a single timestep, the timeout duration, and your own preferences.) Low values for photo_interval can quickly lead to a lot of storage usage by each model’s photos folder. These should either be cleaned out manually from time to time (e.g. once a model is complete) or via a subroutine in run_star_extras.f. The functionality to let MOrPy take care of photo file removal is planned but not yet implemented.

Lastly, the database file (called runs.db in the examples) does not only serve morpy’s tracking capabilities, it also acts as safeguard again accidental data deletion. Once a database file is initialised the contents of previously existing (i.e. registered in the database file) models cannot be overwritten when using the prepare_grid() function. If you want to reinitialise a project directory and its model (work) directories, you should manually remove the database file first, as the RuntimeError you get suggests. Note that this safeguard is only built into the prepare_grid() function (defined in the project_setup module), which uses the user-accessible create_modeldir() function. Know that if you choose to use the latter function yourself with overwrite=True, you might accidentally delete model output if you are not careful.
